utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. And, Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Before we continue the examination of you, Mr. Krajisnik, I have one announcement. From the last session of yesterday a DVD -- a video DVD has been produced and will be handed out to you today so that you can look at it. It has been produced in the B/C/S version. It was considered that that is what you would need. If that would be not the case, then please inform us, and you're invited to look at whether it functions on your computer so that you -- and please report to the Chamber if you can't look at it so that we can try to fix that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have already received the DVDs. Your employees are very prompt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So I'm, perhaps as always, a bit behind the fact. And have you tested it already, Mr. Krajisnik? Not yet. Okay. So then we'll hear from you if it doesn't function. Yes. Then, Mr. Krajisnik, I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration that you've given at the beginning of your testimony yesterday. And, Mr. Stewart, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, we were looking at and I hope you still have a copy in front of you of the transcript of your interview on the television programme, Club 91. You're nodding so I can see that you have that. Where we got to yesterday, do you find in the margin of your copy the number 3?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, this is in the -- almost in the middle of page 4 of the English where Mr. Krajisnik is recorded as saying: "The viewers will see that but I hope you will also recognise that," and then we continue in the transcript. The presenter says: "Mr. Krajisnik, so, to begin - behind us is yesterday's long-running government session at which there was discussion, as you know, viewers, about the problems of regionalisation in Bosnia and Herzegovina. We have all heard the conclusions and there have already been reactions today. Can you tell us your opinion about these problems, yesterday's government session and regionalisation in general?"

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, first of all, you did not personally attend that government session, did you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you -- is it correct you wouldn't have normally attended the government session because you weren't, in fact, a member of the government?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Then I'll go through the answer that you gave on that occasion. You said: "I think it is very difficult to form an answer to this question. Much happened and I think that there are differences as regards regionalisation. I will tell you my personal view, which I think is a duty that I must say from the position of president of the Assembly but talking also as a man and a citizen of this Bosnia and Herzegovina. I unambiguously believe and this was stated at the session of the Assembly and the government itself that according to the Constitution regionalisation is allowed, in fact, it is a voluntary act of the municipalities which want it and which can realise it with their voluntary action if they established that there are political interests. Legally, too, even though there have been objections here, it is unambiguous here that, also legally there is no basis to challenge that."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then, Your Honours, the next two lines are one of those handwritten notes that we can scrub for immediate purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Krajisnik, the question you'd been asked by the presenter included asking your opinion about regionalisation in general. But the question I am putting to you now today is would you tell Your Honours what at this time in this context - this time in 1991 - what was regionalisation?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1991 regionalisation, albeit legally grounded in the constitution, had a certain political dimension as well. It created a rift between parties, between sides. Therefore, it did not have the real basis as designed, as imagined by the writer of the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Let me start with this then, Mr. Krajisnik. Did the three main parties, all three of them, the SDA, the HDZ, and the SDS, have differing approaches to regionalisation at that time, in May 1991?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. They had different approaches.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was there -- just to clarify, was there, to start with, a difference of approach between the SDA and the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps, but it was not a visible difference. If you allow me to explain, HDZ was in favour of regionalisation, whereas SDA was absolutely against it, categorically against it. When I say that the HDZ was in favour of regionalisation, that applied only when it was in the interest of the Croatian people, and that's when they implemented it. As for the Serb side and as for what the Serbs did, then the HDZ was sympathetic with the SDA in their opposition to regionalisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, this is -- if I may comment, this is clearly a potentially complex subject, so just as we go into it I'd invite you to -- to stick to my questions and we'll take it in steps. The -- you've said in your answer there in relation to difference of approach between the SDA and the HDZ, you said: It was not a visible difference. And then I'm not cross-examining you, Mr. Krajisnik, but you, first of all, say it's a visible difference and then you say the HDZ was in favour of regionalisation, whereas the SDA was absolutely against it. That second comment does seem to be rather a sharp difference between them as opposed to you saying there was no visible difference. So would you clarify that. What I'm putting to you is that on your own answer there plainly was a substantial difference between the SDA and the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the agenda featured mainly the regionalisation implemented by the Serbs, and on that issue the HDZ and the SDA were joined against such regionalisation. And when I was trying to explain a moment ago about regionalisation in general and the approaches of the various sides, I said that the SDA was absolutely against it, whereas the HDZ would be in favour of it when it applied to Western Herzegovina, for instance. So one thing happened in the Assembly, and the political moves outside of it was something quite different and we were aware of those political moves. In this interview I was talking only about what was going on at the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Let's then -- let's start, Mr. Krajisnik, with asking you to describe as succinctly as you can the essentials of the SDS policy on regionalisation at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did you mean the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I hoped I said the SDS. I did mean the SDS, Mr. Krajisnik, yes.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The SDS exercised the possibility provided by the constitution to revive the issue of regionalisation which was topical even before the multi-party elections, and it was all legally justified. However, politically it was an answer to the violation of the constitution by two sides concerning the fact that they put their declaration of the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina on the agenda of the Assembly in February 1992 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So, Mr. Krajisnik, what -- leaving aside for one moment whether -- what it was an answer to and the reasons why it was adopted, you've indicated, as an answer, what were the essentials of the regionalisation as a practical policy of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even apart from this first answer, this first reaction, the SDS wanted municipalities to regionalise, it wanted regionalisation to go on, because many regions had been left behind, forgotten, because Sarajevo, as the centre, enjoyed all the advantages. And in order to provide for a polycentric development of Bosnia and Herzegovina, we in the SDS pushed regionalisation for Bosnia and Herzegovina always looking to Switzerland as a model.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When you say that the SDS wanted municipalities to regionalise, then what is it that the SDS wanted the municipalities to do to implement that regionalisation?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: To act according to the constitution. Each municipality was supposed to declare its own will to say whether they wanted to join a particular region if such an initiative existed, and that was carried out in practice. They were only exercising their right given by the constitution to declare what they wanted, which region they wanted to join.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I want just to -- in your answers, please, to try to take these steps in -- in specific detail bit by bit. You say that "each municipality was supposed to declare its own will." By what mechanism was the municipality to declare its own will? What body was to do it? How was it to be done?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The constitution provided the grounds for regionalisation. Under the socialist system it was all orchestrated, whereas we suggested that it should be somehow coordinated and negotiated among representatives of various municipalities. They would meet and agree, and after that each municipality would start an initiative in its own to implement that idea. It was actually only about reviving the regions that had existed earlier, before those multi-party elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So the representatives of the various municipalities that you suggested should somehow coordinate and negotiate among themselves, are you talking about Serbs only or Serbs and representatives from the other nationalities?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not talking only about the Serbs, because various ethnic communities lived in each of the municipalities, Croats, Serbs, and Muslims. I'm talking about adjoining municipalities, contiguous ones. You cannot regionalise municipalities that are far from each other; only contiguous municipalities could form one whole. So a municipality which leaned territorially on to an existing region had the possibility of declaring its will at a referendum and joining that region. That's how it was done in practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And was the intention then, Mr. Krajisnik, that there would eventually be regions that were politically run by Serbs and there would be other regions that were politically run by Muslims or by Croats?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Speaking of regionalisation, at that time there was no thought of unifying only Serb majority municipalities. We have proof in the statement of the president of the then-Serb region of Krajina in which he invited other Muslim majority municipalities to join that region.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So that when you referred to a municipality declaring its will, it was the Municipal Assembly of a particular municipality that would make that decision and declare its will if it wanted to join a particular region. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are quite right. That's the way it went all the way up to the outbreak of armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, may I ask --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- you to seek one clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In this respect Mr. Krajisnik also mentioned, and I read that a municipality had the possibility of declaring its will at a referendum, and I have some difficulties to reconcile a -- the expression of its will by a decision of the Municipal Assembly or by a referendum. That's just unclear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour's absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, your reference to referendum, was that -- was that on the basis that a municipality would hold a referendum before deciding -- well, I'll ask that question first. Was that on the basis that it was expected that a municipality would hold a referendum before a decision was taken?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't actually recall mentioning a referendum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It might be a translation issue. Perhaps we check that during the next break.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. Perhaps if I put the answer to Mr. Krajisnik to see if he does accept it straight away, otherwise we'll look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, what we have -- and I'm reading of course from the English transcript now. What we have a few minutes ago is you saying, first of all, you can't regionalise municipalities that are far from each other, and only contiguous municipalities could form one whole. And then you are recorded on our transcript as having said: "So a municipality which leaned territorially on to an existing region had the possibility of declaring its will at a referendum and joining that region. That's how it was done in practice."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note, if this will be of assistance, I hope, it was a misunderstanding by the interpreter when the -- when Mr. Krajisnik said "declaring its will."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... a moment, please. We'll listen to the interpreter first, if we may.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm so sorry. Thank you, interpreter. Could you just finish what you were saying?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I have finished. I misunderstood Mr. Krajisnik to mean a referendum when he was talking about declaring its will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's been clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you, Madam Interpreter. Excuse me, Your Honour, I'm trying to pick up where we were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Page 8 --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, that's very kind, Your Honour. Perhaps we should clarify what Mr. Krajisnik did say at that point. So is it -- Madam Interpreter, is it -- May I, Your Honour, put that question through the Bench to Madam Interpreter as to what Mr. Krajisnik did actually say at that point?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Everything except "referendum." Declaring its will and joining that region.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the "referendum" was added in the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not actually -- I don't remember saying "referendum."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you are absolutely right about that. It seems to be completely agreed now; it was just a misunderstanding. The -- so it was -- just to summarise. It was to be -- it was for Municipal Assemblies to make the decision. If -- once municipalities -- let's take that -- once municipalities had declared their will to join a particular region, so it's got to be more than one municipality, otherwise you don't have a region. So but once some municipalities have declared their will to join a particular region, what was the SDS expectation as to how that region would then be governed?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Municipalities took their decision like any other decision at Assembly sessions. Since I am under oath to tell the truth, I'm going to say that the SDS only made a political move that would be a reply to the other side to the effect that the Bosnian Herzegovinian crisis should be resolved by agreement instead of imposing a solution. Because even regions should be based on agreement between all three sides, whereas in this respect there was obviously no agreement even about regions among the three sides. So it was a political answer to the self-willed decision-making by the other two sides. It was a signal that we should have an agreement, both about the regions and the solution for Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, could we then stick with the -- first of all, with the question -- the specific question that I asked you. You've -- let's assume you've got a situation where at least a few municipalities have declared their will in the way you've described to join a particular region. What was the SDS expectation as to how that region would then be governed? In other words, in some way above the level of the individual municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I'm not getting translation. Your Honour probably isn't either.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear the English booth now?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now yes. Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course we need some other -- some foreign words to be spoken in order to see whether the translation continues. If you please continue or repeat your question, Mr. Stewart, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, just say something in your language like congratulations on the football or something like that, just anything in your own language.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can say that I can hear all of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krajisnik. So I will put my question again, though, Mr. Krajisnik. You've got a situation where at least a few municipalities have declared their will in the way you've described to join a particular region. What was the SDS expectation as to how that region would then be governed, in other words, in some way above the level of the individual municipalities?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite simply, I'm not saying that that's what the SDS wanted it to be like, but I'm giving you the position of the SDS. These regions were to behave exactly as envisaged by the BH constitution, and what was envisaged was that municipalities could transfer some of their powers to the region. And these powers would be dealt with at the Assembly of the region or the Executive Council of the region. I do not remember what the name was in the constitution. But these bodies would in turn pass decisions which would then be handed down to the municipalities that had been brought together.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And the -- you've indicated that the -- something about the HDZ position. How did the HDZ at that time then, how did they express their position on this process? Did they say that they were overall in favour, or did they say that they were generally against or what was their expression of policy?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, the HDZ was silent. They did not publicly express their views on regionalisation. However, tacitly in the Assembly when there were decisions concerning regionalisation, they would actually express their solidarity with the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And the SDA you have already said were opposed to regionalisation. Did they express, first of all, publicly, did the SDA publicly express reasons for their opposition?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And what reasons did they give?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The SDA interpreted regionalisation to mean the break-up of Bosnia-Herzegovina because they were advocating a unitary firm united sovereign, as they say, Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And when you say, to clarify, at that time were they advocating a unitary -- I beg your pardon. Were they advocating a sovereign Bosnia and Herzegovina as part of a larger state of Yugoslavia or an independent sovereign Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are different stages in which they advocated different things. If you allow me to explain, the SDA in the election campaign advocated Bosnia within Yugoslavia. In the first period after the multi-party elections they advocated Bosnia-Herzegovina in Yugoslavia, a reformed one of course, and then a self-reliant Bosnia-Herzegovina, and then a Bosnia-Herzegovina within Yugoslavia when the historical agreement was reached, and then, yet again, a Bosnia-Herzegovina outside Yugoslavia. And that was the last stage that went on from October 1991 until the beginning of the armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In this time we're talking about, in May 1991, was it your understanding -- and I'm asking specifically about you, Mr. Krajisnik. I'm not talking about the SDS or any larger group. Was it your understanding that the SDA were supporting a continuation of Bosnia and Herzegovina within a larger state of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's hard for me to define what the position of the SDA was, but precisely in that period of time there was a debate on the declaration that was -- this was the declaration concerning a sovereign Bosnia-Herzegovina that was discussed at the constitutional commission and different bodies. And there was an opportunity that an agreement would be reached which would mean a third thing, so that is to say that at that time the SDA was not firmly in favour of Bosnia-Herzegovina being an independent state. However, in all the debates that model was favoured -- or rather, it was promoted because they wanted the declaration to be adopted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But Mr. Krajisnik, you -- you have -- in your answers this morning to the Trial Chamber, you have indicated that the SDS policy of regionalisation was an answer, as you put it, to the policies of positions of the other parties. That's correct. That's what you have said. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. At the moment when -- or rather, exactly from March until May, up to May, that was the political move concerned. However, the -- when the SDS wanted a recommendation to be put forth at the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina to stop regionalisation until a political solution is found in Bosnia-Herzegovina and for as long as the negotiations go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, the -- in describing regionalisation as an answer, what was the problem to which it was an answer? Let me put it this way: What did the SDS see as the negative aspects of the other parties' policies which could then be met by regionalisation?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In February 1991, the SDA proposed the declaration at the Assembly. There were 20 signatures by SDS deputies, and it was sent to the Council. In these discussions that took place, the SDA position became clear, but what particularly called for regionalisation was a statement made by Mr. Izetbegovic unwittingly at a meeting that was held in Split, a meeting of the presidents of the republic. He said the declaration will be adopted regardless of whether the SDS agrees or not. Then everything followed, that is to say, giving a political response to regionalisation. There is a document that includes this statement made by Mr. Izetbegovic. There is a newspaper article as to what he stated after the Split meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- I'd like to clarify one matter. Page 5, lines 20 and following, I'll read them to Mr. Krajisnik. Mr. Krajisnik, it has been translated to us, and it -- I doubt on whether this is what you said or whether you misspoke. You said: "However, politically," you were talking about regionalisation, "it was an answer to the violation of the constitution by two sides concerning the fact that they put their declaration of the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina on the agenda of the Assembly in February 1992," whereas you are now referring in relation to -- to what the regionalisation was a response, you're referring to 1991. Did you intend to say February 1992 in your earlier answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1991 is the year. 1991. Maybe it was a slip of the tongue, maybe I misspoke, but it was in 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I just sought to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. I should have picked that up at the time, but that's absolutely right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I formulated a question for myself, and since you revisited the matter I thought clarification now would be better.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. That's most helpful, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, the -- we can -- we can look out these documents as necessary, but the -- the key point about Mr. Izetbegovic's statement at that time was what?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The key point of Mr. Izetbegovic's statement when he did not exercise caution, if I can put it that way, was that the Assembly procedure was there, that the declaration was there in the Assembly procedure, and that it would be adopted regardless of whether the SDS agreed to it or not. That was a signal to the effect that all these debates that we had with the representatives of the other two sides in the Assembly procedure -- well, that their position is clear. That they will want that declaration to be carried through, that they would advocate an independent Bosnia-Herzegovina. That sounded off an alarm that we were debating things for no reason whatsoever, because their position was quite clear. I'm trying to be brief, and perhaps my answers are, therefore, not very clear. I can give lengthier answers, but I would like my attorney to lead me and then perhaps I can give shorter answers so that will do. I mean, the questions can be phrased that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What a very good idea. Shall we do it exactly that way. Mr. Krajisnik, the -- the key point -- yes. The key point of the declaration then independent -- or the statement, rather, of Mr. Izetbegovic, independence, Mr. Krajisnik, you may think this is all very obvious after we've been here for about two years, but why did that point require steps to the taken by the SDS and the Serbs as an answer?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at the Assembly in 1991, that is to say in February, Mr. Izetbegovic also made a statement that meant that he was not exactly exercising caution, that he would sacrifice peace for a sovereign Bosnia-Herzegovina. And that showed quite clearly what the intentions of the other two sides were. Just another small addition. A month before that in January 1991 at the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mr. Izetbegovic came out to explain a platform that he was advocating on behalf of Bosnia-Herzegovina with the other presidents of the other republics where he said: I advocate a Bosnia within Yugoslavia; of course a reformed Yugoslavia. And he was applauded by all of those present, and this meant a great deal of relief in the general public. Only a month later the same side, the same man, made a different statement which caused a reaction, the one that I spoke about, that now the SDS sought a political response to. So all of that was involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Krajisnik, the -- and if I may, in a sense, address the Trial Chamber as well. Throughout the whole of the period during which -- with which this case is primarily concerned, and certainly 1991 and early 1992, there were from time to time, weren't there, quite sharp fluctuations in the message that was coming from the SDA about their attitude towards independence of Bosnia. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And is this, without, I hope, leading improperly -- once the SDA at some point had indicated a wish for independence, subsequent swings back in the other direction away from independence were really not sufficiently reassuring to the Bosnian Serbs. Is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the answer is both yes and no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, give the yes first, Mr. Krajisnik, then and then the no. That's probably the best way of dealing with it.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since those were very hard times, even a small positive, favourable statement became a major one and would lead to an alleviation of the situation, as if somebody had pressed a button. So just a small positive statement made by the SDA would bring about a general easing, a general relaxation. If a different statement were made, as soon as a different statement would be made, then the reaction was different, as if the first thing had never happened in the first place. That is why I'm saying yes and no. Because practically the situation changed from one day to another on different grounds. So this complex situation has to be understood. Perhaps no one can understand it because it was so dynamic that even I myself cannot remember all the details sometimes. I beg your pardon, when I'm talking about the SDA -- can I just add something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: His Honour is indicating "yes," Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's part of your answer, so if Mr. Stewart would like otherwise he will give you the guidance, but please add what you would like to add.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm talking now here as if I were accusing the SDA and Mr. Izetbegovic. I must say that the driving force that was instigating the SDA was the HDZ. This is my personal opinion. Had the SDA pursued their independent policy, had they not been instigated I think they would have made moves that were a lot more reasonable. I know Mr. Izetbegovic personally, too, and I know that many times he wanted to achieve something and he could not do it because there were pressures coming from the other side. But that's a different story altogether. I'm saying this for the sake of the truth. I don't want it to appear that I'm not telling the entire truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So, Mr. Krajisnik, that was the "yes" part of your answer. I had asked you a question to which you said the answer was yes or no, and that was your yes part. And no -- just to remind you -- the question was really where there -- when there was swings back away from a policy of independence by the SDA you had said that that might lead to a general easing, but on the no side? On the negative side? Were there ways in which it wasn't sufficiently reassuring, or it didn't ease the situation sufficiently?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: When a people, a nation, are in a difficult situation, then misinformation is bandied about, too. And if a positive statement is made by the SDA, then it seems that somebody says, on purpose: Well, they're just playing both sides. There are some people who are skeptical and some people who believe misinformation and who say: Well, he just said it for political reasons and it's not true. And that is why I said that perhaps it's a yes or no answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So, Mr. Krajisnik, so far as the SDS were led to have concern that the SDA would pursue policy of independence, essentially why was that a problem for the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were all fearing a conflict, not to say a war. You know, we have a tradition. Every person who is born in Bosnia knew that if the three sides don't agree, that's not a good thing. And knowing that the SDA represented the most numerous people, we knew that if they don't agree with something that's not good. And that's why we were concerned, we were worried, not about the vote but worried generally that things might get out of control. And that's why we were worried if the SDA was against something. If it had been a small party representing a small community, a small minority, that would have been different. But SDA representing a very major portion of the people, their opinion had a weight.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, for the purposes of these questions now, I want to start by drawing, I hope, a clear distinction between two things so we understand the basis of the question. If you had one nation that wanted independence and you had another nation -- I'm leaving aside for the moment the fact that there were three nations, but if you had one nation that wanted independence and another nation that didn't and they were sufficiently determined, there was the prospect of a civil war. That -- that's clear, isn't it, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that it was absolutely crystal clear to everybody in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But my question first, my prior question, is intended to, if you like, move back a step from that, Mr. Krajisnik. Why was the prospect of independent Bosnia and Herzegovina itself unacceptable to the Serbs which then led them to oppose it so strongly?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a number of reasons. First, because somebody would be abolishing a state overnight. We had Yugoslavia at the time. Second, because the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina was being pursued through unconstitutional means and not everybody was equally committed to a compromise. Instead, the other side, the coalition between the SDA and the HDZ, the two sides that agreed, they were willing to have Bosnia and Herzegovina out of Yugoslavia without being choosey about the means. And when I say "without being choosey," I mean pursuing an illegal, unconstitutional road, whereas we wanted a legal, constitutional position that would allow for a compromise, which was what actually happened when the international community got involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But, Mr. Krajisnik, what was it about living in an independent Bosnia and Herzegovina as it was structured before regionalisation that was inherently unacceptable to the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will voice my opinion, and I believe that it is shared by an overwhelming majority of Serbs. First of all, the Muslim side said: We won't stay in Yugoslavia because we're afraid to stay together with Serbs as a minority. And the reaction of the Serbs was: If you are afraid of having us as a majority in a common state, then how can we trust you, to be together with you as a minority if you are already acting unconstitutionally within Yugoslavia? What would you do if you were a majority then? We thought that Yugoslavia was the best solution because all the "problematic" communities, Muslims and Croats and others, would be together in one state. Of course it applied to us Serbs as well. We would be in one state without borders together with all the other Serbs, but so would others, Muslims and Croats. That was our approach. Maybe there was some other reasons, too, but those were the primary reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Is this correct, Mr. Krajisnik, that if you -- and I'm here talking about the SDS, if you had been confident that come what may Bosnia and Herzegovina would remain part of Yugoslavia, regionalisation would have been unnecessary from the SDS viewpoint?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We believed -- I often use the word "we" because I don't like to say "I." And when I say "we," I mean the SDS. We believed that it was necessary to reshape both Yugoslavia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. But to answer your question, if this regionalisation was in dispute, if Bosnia stayed within Yugoslavia, regionalisation itself would be automatically eliminated and that solution was already within reach under one of the plans that had been developed. I learned to use the word "Muslims" rather than "Bosniaks" a long time ago, and I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So, Mr. Krajisnik, the -- you mentioned earlier that policy of regionalisation was seen by the SDA as the break-up of Bosnia and Herzegovina, or leading to the break-up of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Did -- did the SDS view regionalisation as in any sense the break-up of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will answer, if you allow me, with a small addition. SDS did not consider that as a break-up of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and it wasn't, and it could not have been. The SDA was not right about that, and if you allow me to add. The SDA ruled the -- in the unregionalised Bosnia and Herzegovina in a great number of municipality which had a large percentage of Serbs and they wanted domination. In their eyes, regionalisation was taking away from the power of the centre of Sarajevo, giving more power to the regional level. The SDA represented the majority people, and regionalisation diminished their power to rule. And their desire to rule was evident at the republic level in Bosnia and Herzegovina and it was also quite obvious on the local level.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was it -- was it the SDS policy that, provided cooperation could be achieved from the other parties, there would, as part of this regionalisation process, be some regions which were under the control of the Muslims or, in some parts of the country, Croats?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't think I understood the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, would -- did the SDS policy contemplate that as the regionalisation process proceeded, some regions would be under the control of Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. We were not against regionalising all of Bosnia and Herzegovina, so the answer is: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And some regions would be under control of Croats, would they?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did -- did such a policy include any expectation that there would be significant population movements as a consequence?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. You can see that in one shorthand note where I gave a statement. Nobody was supposed to move from their location. Somebody would be in the majority in one region, another side would be in the majority in another region. But nobody was supposed to move, and it was a complete fallacy. Nobody was advocating any moves of the population, at least not that I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, the -- we started here with a reference to the Club 91 interview which had referred to a long-running government session the previous day. What had been the outcome of that government session?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The government, as far as I remember now, made a decision contrary to the decision of the Assembly concerning regionalisation; namely, as far as I remember, the government's decision on regionalisation was negative. Maybe it was not a ban but it was contrary to the recommendation of the Assembly. The government, conditionally speaking, made a decision to ban, or to forbid - I don't remember the exact wording - but it was formulated in an imperative, obligatory way, negatively.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, could you find, returning to the transcript of the -- of your television interview, could you find the number 5, please, in the margin?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, this is right in the middle of page 5 of the English transcript where there's a paragraph beginning: "I did not like the way." Do Your Honours see that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, we have got a passage in the English transcript which begins, I hope you can pick it up against the number 5: "I did not like the way in which regionalisation was included on the Assembly's agenda." Do you see that sentence in the -- your own language? Thank you. So you say: "I did not like the way in which regionalisation was included on the Assembly's agenda. I think that was a mistake, as well. First of all, the question was created that this was regionalisation ... The municipalities of Bosnian Krajina were separating and joining the Serbian Autonomous District or Region Krajina. That was included in the Assembly so alarmingly that I was appalled." Mr. Krajisnik, could you -- could you clarify, please, what -- what was the mistake -- what it was you were appalled by at that point?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that Assembly session was in June. I don't remember exactly. That Assembly session first adopted its agenda, and there was a debate that did not include regionalisation. And suddenly an SDA representative comes out bringing news that an agreement was included by SAO Krajina and Bosnian Krajina and the Bosnian Krajina was leaving Bosnia and Herzegovina and joining Yugoslavia. And he wanted it included in the agenda, although the agenda had already been adopted. So we continued to discuss regionalisation, although it was not part of the agenda, and that representative, that deputy, put it to others in a very alarming way: Bosnian Krajina is leaving now. And that group of deputies presented it in such a way that it caused great concern to the Muslim side. That's the way that they infiltrated this issue into the agenda. After all the discussions and all the debate about the agenda, after the agenda was adopted, and it was completely against all rules of procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So you -- you say that that particular representative, that deputy -- do you remember who that was that conveyed that news to the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was Mr. Irfan Ajanovic. I think. But that can be checked in the transcript of that Assembly session that adopted the recommendation on regionalisation. You can see from those notes exactly how that issue came to be debated. When the recommendation was adopted to include that in the agenda, you can see how it was done, and I think it was Mr. Irfan Ajanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krajisnik, continuing to ask you to give the Trial Chamber your recollection of these events, you said that that particular deputy, whether it was that particular man, conveyed or discussed this matter in a very alarming way. So you're saying, Mr. Krajisnik, are you, that there was -- there was some gap or difference between what was actually happening in relation to the Bosnian Krajina and what the Assembly was being led to understand by this particular deputy. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. There was a gap, a big gap.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, can you explain that gap, Mr. Krajisnik? In other words, compare what was actually happening with the way it was presented to the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Grahovo, late Milan Babic met with several MPs from the Bosnian Assembly who were Serbs from Banja Luka, and they prepared a communique presenting an idea for the Serbian Krajina to join with the Serbian Autonomous District in Croatia. It was no Assembly decision. It was not a -- an authoritative body that took that decision, it was just an idea. And the way it was presented, it was very dramatic, like something that was being done behind our backs. And it was, actually, behind our backs because none of us were aware of that intention. And the comment, which was very important, was that by this act the Bosnian Krajina was being taken away from Bosnia and annexed to Serbia. If a part of Bosnia was being taken away, that was of great concern to everybody, of course. And that just added fuel to the already-existing tensions in the -- in the Assembly that were running high. It was very difficult to lead that session. I'm just summing up all that this deputy said. I can't remember exactly whether it was Cengic or Ajanovic, but one of the two said that the dramatic tone in which it was presented was unbelievable, especially to the viewers who were following that session. And I particularly didn't like the way it was being included in the agenda. We were practically finishing one session and starting a new session. If they had only waited for the new session to begin, we could have done everything according to the rules of procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You said in that answer, Mr. Krajisnik, that it was actually behind your backs because none of you were aware of that intention. When -- when this particular matter was brought up by this particular deputy, whoever exactly it was, are you saying that you personally did not know whether what the Assembly was being told was accurate or not?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was absolutely unaware. I didn't know that it happened at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So, returning to what you say in the interview, about six lines into that passage that we were looking at, you said: "That was included in the Assembly so alarmingly that I was appalled. I thought that, this is it, this is the moment when Bosnia and Herzegovina disappears, Yugoslavia disappears, there will be war," and so on. So you're telling the viewers of the television programme what your reaction had been in the Assembly. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And what -- what was it, as specifically as you can tell the Trial Chamber, that led you to that view at that moment, that Bosnia and Herzegovina would disappear, Yugoslavia will disappear, there will be war?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how this text is understood, but when you see a man talking about something in a very dramatic tone and you are not in the know at that moment, one Krajina is leaving the state and joining another, Bosnia is being broken up, I can say that the way he's talking, the way I hear it, it's so dramatic that the war will begin any moment now. I'm just trying to explain how he was talking about it. I didn't believe at that time that the war was imminent. I was just saying that -- just hearing him talk, one had no choice but to believe that Bosnia was about to cease to exist and the war was about to begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then you continue in the interview. The next sentence after that you say: "As time went by, I think that ... and what happened yesterday in the Assembly ... in the government, I think that was a mistake in one basic approach. That is to say, I have now heard that ... the reactions which have come from the Bosnian Krajina, from Herzegovina, and from other regions, have in fact been ignored. Just as they were ignored regarding the recommendation, they were ignored on such decisions of the government." What -- ignored by whom?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And -- well, which municipality were ...

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, those municipalities that were involved in regionalisation, that had joined a region, because the government passed a decision abolishing regions, and those municipalities were disregarding, going against their decision. And I was saying that it was a very bad thing that we had a situation in which municipalities did not honour, did not observe, the decisions of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then you say: "So it is good if the government is not divided and there is no out-voting, that was positive last night, and I think that everyone should assess that from their own point of view." What was the particular point from the previous night, by which clearly means the government session, doesn't it -- well, perhaps we had better confirm that. When you say "that was positive last night," you are referring to the government session, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And what was it particularly that you were describing there as positive?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the government passed that decision through out-voting, that is, without the consent of Serb ministers. And I was saying here that that was not a good thing. Another bad thing was that the way it was taken, that government's decision was impossible to implement because every decision impossible to implement was showing the public that the state was impotent, and it was the fact that the Assembly's recommendations were not followed that brought the state into that situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So the positive -- the positive point was what?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm saying here is that it is positive when the government stands united, when there is no out-voting within the government. So the word "positive" here pertains to my own opinion that it is a good thing when the government is a monolithic one because it consists of the representatives of three different peoples. The word "positive" applies to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Well, perhaps to clarify, Mr. Krajisnik, it seems that what's happened here, whether it's a translation point, that you were not, in fact, saying in this television programme that there had been anything positive the previous night. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Nothing happened. I'm just giving a comment, that it's a good thing when there is no out-voting within a government and that that is positive, and then I continue to say what is negative. It would have been positive had there been no out-voting, but that was not the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, is that positively time for a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This would be a -- if this would be a suitable moment for you, it would be for the Chamber as well. We'll adjourn until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, on that transcript that you have, could you find the number 6, please, in the margin?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, this is at page 6 of the English transcript, the first intervention by the presenter: "We will certainly get to that subject," it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you have that number 6, Mr. Krajisnik? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The presenter says this: "We will certainly get to that subject. I think that this is a key -- it is a key issue, but I would only ask you to answer this - as regards regionalisation the Serbian Democratic Party is being accused of wanting to divide up Bosnia and Herzegovina according to the 'Knin method' and place its sovereignty on, and I quote, 'the sacrificial alter of a Greater Serbia.'" Mr. Krajisnik, how did you understand at that time the Knin method?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Serb autonomous province of Krajina, that's in Croatia, municipalities declared their own positions and they made up these autonomous regions by uniting certain municipalities. This was also a political response in Croatia. And now a parallel is being drawn to what was going on in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And was there a distinction between the Knin method and the method of regionalisation contemplated by the SDS in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a big difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What was that difference?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because in Croatia this happened through the use of force, that is to say, that there was a conflict, and that is how it was being resolved, whereas in Republika Srpska -- well, another thing. I don't know how they regulated things constitutionally, but in Bosnia-Herzegovina this was going on and beforehand it was only done also in accordance with the constitution exclusively. And it relied upon what happened in socialism before the multi-party elections, whereas over there it was just a defence mechanism against the Croatian regime that threw the Serbs out of the constitution and they used to be in the constitution as a constituent people.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And the reference there in the presenter's question or comment on -- to the "sacrificial alter of a Greater Serbia," at that time was the concept of a Greater Serbia any part of SDS policy?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The notion of a Greater Serbia was used in election campaigns by a certain number of people, but the platform of the SDS was never a Greater Serbia, if I can call it that way. Even if I were to be asked today what it meant I would have great difficulty in explaining it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That was going to be my next question, Mr. Krajisnik, so you've headed it off. But could you do your best then, despite the great difficulty. My question is precisely what -- what did you understand at the time to be meant by those who did campaign for a Greater Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm just going to make a small correction. What those who accused Serbs of wanting a Greater Serbia meant, that is what I'm going to tell you about. Through this accusation that the Serbs were advocating a Greater Serbia, they meant and were saying that the Serbs wanted to expand Serbia now to Serb ethnic lands outside Serbia and to take areas that did not belong to Serb ethnic areas, that is to say that they wanted to create a Greater Serbia, a Serbia bigger than the existing one. This was used in a pejorative sense, in a negative sense, and that was something that they did not have the right to do. It is linked to an agreement that was reached a long time ago at the London conference, and this was being imputed to the Serbs all the time that they were trying to take something that did not belong to them and to create a greater state -- a Greater Serbia, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The -- was there -- were there among the Bosnian Serbs - and I'm talking about those who were politically active, Mr. Krajisnik - were there among the politically active Bosnian Serbs any who did speak in favour of a Greater Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one advocated a Greater Serbia, but that word was used often by people who wanted to be radical and to explain something that would be in their view positive for the Serbs, but that was not the concept, one of a Greater Serbia, and that can be seen by the sequence of events that followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: If you would find number 8 in the margin, please, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's -- Your Honours, we're going on to the page now -- that's on page 9 of the English, the first reference to

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: "I have to say that every party ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, do you find number 8?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I'll give the presenter's short passage first. The presenter says: "Yes, but in the meantime, they scare each other ... the parties, or they get scared or we scare them, for example, by saying that it is someone's aim to create an independent state of Croatia; that someone is thoroughly and quietly preparing a Muslim state; that someone, again, is keeping the others in some Serboslavia or a Greater Serbia. Are these phantom categories or real options in your opinion?" And then you say: "I have to say that every party has a left and a right wing and centre. And that right wing, to call it that, that right-oriented wing is promoting a Greater Serbia, in fact, they promote an Islamic state of Bosnia and Herzegovina, a third group promotes a confederation or a Greater Croatia or an NDH, independent state of Croatia, and want some kind of national" -- Just pausing there to seek clarification, because it's perhaps not a hundred per cent clear in English anyway, you're saying that -- is this right: You're saying that right wing, that there are right wings in the three parties. The right-oriented wing of the SDS is promoting a Greater Serbia; the right-oriented wing of the SDA is promoting an Islamic state; and the right-oriented wing of the HDZ is promoting a confederation or a Greater Croatia or an independent state of Croatia? Is that a correct summary of what you are saying there, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, please correct that summary, then, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, the right wing in a party accused the others, say the right wing of the SDS accused others of creating an NDH or an Islamic state. Among them there were some who said: If they don't want to be with us, we're going to create a Greater Serbia. So that was the rhetoric involved. The others from the SDA, the right wing of the SDA, would say: Well, you in the SDS wanted to create a Greater Serbia, a Serboslavia, we don't want to be there. And among them there were people who said: We want to have our own state, we want Bosnia-Herzegovina to be our own state, even to have Islamic laws. In the HDZ the situation was rather specific. From the very outset they officially advocated a confederal Bosnia -- sorry, Yugoslavia, a confederal Yugoslavia. As for Bosnia, they officially advocated independent Bosnia-Herzegovina only to get it out of Yugoslavia, and they believed that in the stage that would follow they would manage either to regionalise their own areas or to annex them to Croatia. If I were to be sincere, on all three sides there were accusations leveled at the others and also promoting certain negative ideas in terms of one's own programme. That is as far as extremist views go.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: How -- how prevalent, if they were prevalent, how prevalent were such views within the membership of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At big meetings, different views were heard, and if we were to go through all of that there were such statements made in public, too. However, the conclusions reached and the official policy were quite clear. First of all, that we should remain in Yugoslavia; and later that there should be a transformation of Bosnia and Herzegovina in which we were to have a constituent unit of our own.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In this answer here at -- well, it's point 8, the marking you've got on your transcript, then just carrying on from where I stopped reading it goes on about five lines in: "So that Bosnia is a nation state of one people with, perhaps, superiority over the others." You're reporting views of various factions there. "I think that that is not the basic rule, that is not -- that is not the basic concept of any party ..." So among other things, Mr. Krajisnik, you're saying it's not the basic view of any party that an Islamic state should be promoted. Was that genuinely your view at that time, that the SDA policy did not involve promotion of an Islamic state of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was only the SDA that could have advocated that option. They were the most numerous people. And due to the birth rate there they would have easily reached the figure of 51 per cent, so it would have been their state, demographically speaking. However, from contacts with the SDA, from conversations with the SDA, on several occasions I was convinced that they were really at a crossroads. Perhaps they wanted that, to have only a state of their own, but they would like to have a compromised solution because they know what the specific characteristics of Bosnia are and they want peace. Now, I am saying what they were saying in our conversations; what they were saying when they were talking on their own is something that I don't know. I know what they said in public, too, when certain people said that the Serbs have Serbia, the Croats have Croatia, and that this is our state. However, I had the impression that in conversations for a long time they aspired for a rational, compromised solution. There were ups and downs, that is to say. Of course people from our party accused them, just like they were accusing us, but that was political rhetoric to my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, there's a -- on the fourth line --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, just a moment. But for sure, had there been an independent Bosnia, in our view, due to the birth rate, it would have become a predominantly Muslim state soon, so this was just an addition I wanted to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, on the fourth line of that answer, that's line 10 on page 36, the phrase appears "demographically speaking," Mr. Sladojevic tells me and I trust the interpreters would agree that it was perhaps democratically. Perhaps we can seek clarification.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters believe that Mr. Krajisnik said demographically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Both make sense, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, that's why I raise it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you said, Mr. Krajisnik, that they would have easily reached the figure of 51 per cent, so it would have been their state, did you say "demographically speaking" or did you say "democratically speaking"? Both could make sense, but what did you say? There's some dispute about what you said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my statement now I said "demographically," birth rate; and before that I said that it's democratic, too. If you have 51 per cent it's democratic as well, if you have the 51 per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The matter has been clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the explanation is the words sound very similar in Serbian as well. Something of course I know. That's what I'm told anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's what happens if they are classical quotes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. So, Mr. Krajisnik, can we go, please, to point 10. It's very shortly afterwards; it's probably over the next page on your copy, but it's page 10 of the English. It's a long answer or comment from you in the interview. So, Mr. Krajisnik, it starts: "As regards a referendum." But, Your Honours, Mr. Krajisnik, I want to go just beyond halfway through that answer unless anybody tells me I should -- ought to go somewhere else. "We should not be politically blind." Do you see a sentence that begins in that way, Mr. Krajisnik? It's just over halfway down that --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You do, thank you. "We should not be politically blind, to not see obviously that one people wants to remain in one state, that is the Serbian people, the Muslim people wants an independent Bosnia, an autonomous Bosnia, the Croatian people wants a confederation and that these two options - a confederation and an independent Bosnia - happen to correspond." Mr. Krajisnik, could you just explain what you understood at that time to be a -- a confederation to be?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time the official policy of the republics that had separated from Yugoslavia was advocating a confederation, so all the states would be independent, but there would just be this umbrella of a confederation. This is what Mr. Tudjman advocated, this is what the Croatian side in Bosnia advocated. So in this way Bosnia would also become independent basically as a state. All these states would actually have very loose ties at an all-Yugoslav level.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Could we move on then, please -- we'll go right on, please, to where you find the number 13 in the margin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And for us, Mr. Stewart?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. It's -- it's against the word "jingle" on page 19, toward the top. We won't play the jingle, Your Honour, we'll spare you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, it's actually -- that's the point of reference. But if we go a bit further down, the presenter is saying -- two answers from you on that page, and then the presenter says: "You see, we have an awful lot of questions from viewers," this was a phone-in programme. We can see that on the video, actually. "I would ask you, let us start, if we have dealt with any of that we won't go back. Hasan Brkic, a journalist in Tesanj, asks you: What fund is being used to pay for arming the Bosnian Serbs with Kragujevac weapons? Do you know anything about that?" And you say: "I don't know, I think they are being armed, but if such a fund exists then really ... I think that the question is more of a provocative one." You're saying you think they are being armed. These are Bosnian Serbs. Which Bosnian Serbs were you referring to there that you thought were being armed?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer here was to a provocative question. I gave a provocative answer to a provocative question, because if somebody asks me as if it were a fact, Serbs are being armed and with what funds, and then I said: Well, yes, they are being armed. Of course I was being provocative. I answered -- I gave a political answer because if somebody is telling me they are being armed, they are asking the president of the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina whether they are being armed, that is to say that this person is saying that he knows that I know. So it was put in provocative terms. Maybe here it looks as if I said it seriously, but later on there are similar answers, too, because somebody is making -- it's not that somebody is putting a question to me, but this person is making an assertion saying: They are being armed, and then putting a question on the basis of that. I did not know that they were being armed. I could just assume that all peoples were being armed because that later became evident when the war broke out.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: If we can go on to point 14 which is -- it will be -- well, on everybody's version it will be at least a couple of pages on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's at page 22 of the English transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Presenter -- towards the top of the page, page 22, Mr. Krajisnik, right against 14 in the margin the presenter says: "Regionalisation - many questions - let us see, could ... is it true that by going to Pale you contributed to Pale being joined to the Romanija region?" That's a viewer from Pale asking that question. And you say: "I think that's provocative. As the president of the Assembly, I would never be against the recommendation nor would I influence regionalisation. The people have done that themselves." Mr. Krajisnik, there was some specific visit you have made to Pale that was included in this viewer's question, was there?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That viewer was making an allusion to a visit, but I don't remember ever being in Pale except on a students' class trip just before the war when an Assembly session was held there. It's not that I didn't take part in it; I simply don't remember ever having been in Pale. And I absolutely don't understand which meeting was alluded to. I did not take part in the regionalisation at Pale nor did I attend any such meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Is it right, Mr. Krajisnik, at this time in May 1991 you had -- you had no personal connection with Pale?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, that's correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Except when somebody would come to the Assembly. But I absolutely didn't go to Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Then it's just -- do you find 15, number 15, in the margin?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, I want to go just above that to the point where Mr. Krajisnik says: "No kind of repressive measures are advisable." And then the presenter says immediately after that: "Why are the municipalities of the Krajina" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which page?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Oh, so sorry, Your Honour. Page 23, top of the page, about -- well, it's four items down: "Why are the municipalities of the Krajina and Herzegovina separating? This separating, it probably means - creating their own region and not separating," that's a question from a viewer in Mostar. And you say: "They are not separating and they are staying in Bosnia and Herzegovina and they will certainly not make any states because that is now solely the reason for this situation but if that were to acquire a political character I think that that can only be if we do not pay attention to ... preserving this state of ours and if we want to break it up."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, first of all, Mr. Krajisnik, was it -- was that, in fact, your -- your genuine understanding of the position at that time that the Krajina and Herzegovina would not separate and would stay in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was my position, that was my view, and I would have been strongly opposed to anybody leaving Bosnia and being annexed to whatever else. That was in May 1991, and that was -- that continued to be my position all the way up to the beginning of the war and even a bit later.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Who was it who would have been in a position to decide at that time whether -- let's take Krajina, whether the Krajina municipalities would separate?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you just give me some leeway to give a broader answer. Krajina is a territorial area that is partly in Croatia and partly in Bosnia and Herzegovina. It was created during the Ottoman and Austro-Hungarian empires, and it was a persisting aspiration of their people to be together. When democracy came, there were several attempts to unite these two parts into one whole, even into one state. We politicians were opposed, not because we were opposing their view but because it was against the Vance Plan and it ran counter to our theory that Bosnia should be a recognised state, and we had a lot of problems dealing with that burning desire of the people. They thought we didn't understand them, and they accused us of trying to work against them. But even if that entity were to be created, it would have been impossible to recognise because it ran counter to all the existing plans. It would not have been possible to implement like the Vance Plan in Croatia. It was simply not realistic politically speaking. Desires and aspirations are one thing and reality is quite another.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Does that answer you've just given apply equally to Herzegovina or are there differences?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Almost in the same terms, with a small difference. Part of Herzegovina, by decision of the Berlin Congress was given to Montenegro, and the people of Herzegovina are very similar to those of Montenegro but they have a Serb orientation. And their desire to join Montenegro was more subdued than in the Serb Krajina in Bosnia and in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now returning to the --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about the people, the communities. I'm talking about the desire of the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Returning to the transcript, point 15 -- well, we've been using point 15 as the reference point, so if we go down, it's page 23, Your Honours, of the English text. Right in the middle of the page it's against -- number 15 in your copy, Mr. Krajisnik, middle of page 23. The presenter asks: "Asim from Sarajevo wants to know: Is the regionalisation that the Serbs are carrying out in the Banja Luka Krajina honest?" And your answer is: "That, honest, is disputable. It is economically justified." I'm not entirely sure from the English there, Mr. Krajisnik. What was the implication that it might be dishonest? Could you explain in what sense it might have been suggested that the regionalisation being carried out by the Serbs was dishonest?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can try to guess what the viewer meant. The viewer thought that in those municipalities where decisions were taken to join certain municipalities, Muslims and Croats had been out-voted, just as Serbs had been out-voted, perfectly legally, in the parliament. There's only one difference. On the regional level it is all according to the law; whereas at the republican level there is a constitutional provision against out-voting. Now, he as a Muslim is asking: Is it fair to go on with this regionalisation wherein you are out-voting us? And I'm answering: Yes, economically it is good, but if it acquires a nationalist -- a national dimension, it is not good because it would only add fuel to the flames and lead to war. And that is how I am understanding his question and trying to answer it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The -- you say then that: "It's economically justified, but I think we must make a lot of efforts so that it does not have negative national consequences." What sort of negative consequences did you have in mind there?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I meant just what I explained just a moment ago. At that time everything had a political dimension, everything was politicised. If you go forward with an economic regionalisation, like in Krajina which was very underdeveloped, and it is viewed by other sides as Serbs coming together against them, then it would have very negative consequences. Because everything that was done by anyone was viewed at that time through a political prism.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
