utterances.text: And then further down, just about ten lines further down, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, it's the third item from the bottom on page 23. The presenter says: "Sinan from Zenica," a viewer, obviously, raising a question. The viewer says: "I have a high opinion of you personally but are you identifying yourself with the so-called Duke Seselj?" And you say: "Thank you, Sinan, for your high opinion, but I think that it is not all right to identify me with Seselj." What at that time was Seselj -- who was he and what was he up to that you did not identify with?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this point I was talking about what Sinan, the viewer, was implying. He saw Seselj as a nationalist, oriented against Muslims, and I answered that I don't want to be identified with him in that way. Seselj was a very intelligent man, and he wasn't the person that Muslims took him for. In that way, I didn't want to be compared with him. I didn't even want to be compared with the US president or anybody else. But on this particular point I didn't want to be identified with Seselj. Otherwise, I had meetings with Seselj and he made a good impression on me, and I thought he was a different man from the one that Muslims saw. But that's quite a different issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, I wish to leave that Club 91 interview and transcript now, please. Excuse me one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, I want to refer to a document which we -- isn't among those scanned and available, so we have hard copies of this. Your Honour, it's called -- in English it's called: "Decision on the establishment of a Serb National Council." Its ERN number is SA04-1938 to 1939.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say it's not scanned. Has it been exhibited before?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: To be frank, I'm not a hundred per cent -- oh, yes it has, Your Honours. Yes. It's there in Mr. Treanor's exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can't give Your Honour immediately the tab and volume number in Mr. Treanor's exhibits, but it is there, it is there, if it's helpful, Your Honour. We -- no doubt we can identify the precise location for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've got a note that it is exhibited in Treanor, so that's my note which I must have got it from somewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That means that it should be somewhere in P64.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The registrar tells me that on the basis of his latest list it's most likely in P64, tab 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, sorry, I could have said it was in P64, but I sort of -- we live and breathe P64 sometimes. We've got it, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's proceed. We'll find where it is just for purposes of reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, it is in tab 15, Your Honour. We -- well, there's a reference to TR428A, but for the life of me I forget what that signifies. But if it's of help, it's on Mr. -- well, whether it's his personally but Mr. Haider's exhibit list. Yes, it is his personally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We should sufficiently locate it to continue. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. But we've produced copies in Mr. Krajisnik's own language as well as English.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, this is jogging back just a short way in time from this -- that Club 91 interview, because this is a document which bears the date 8th of April, 1991. It's not a very long document, Mr. Krajisnik. You've probably been casting your eye over it anyway, but if you would just -- just cast your eye over it to familiarise yourself. Let us know when you've done that.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, were you personally involved in any way in any meeting that led to this decision?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't involved in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you know -- well, first of all, do you know whether there was a meeting that led to this decision?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Therefore -- well, what do you know?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know much, but I will tell you what I know. An initiative came from parties in Serbia, Montenegro, and I believe Bosnia and Herzegovina - I'm not sure whether there was some from Croatia as well - for a political council to be created that would formulate the national or ethnic interests and simply present them as the will of the Serbian people in a broader area. So these parties met in Belgrade, as I learned later. Some were there and some that are listed here walked out of that meeting and didn't sign the document and even some rough language was used to the effect who was the greater patriot, et cetera. But this body was unable to function in practice, and I never felt any of its work in practice. And I'm seeing this document for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I seek one clarification. You're referring to this document as a decision being adopted and immediately --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it says "draft," Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I wanted to give Mr. Krajisnik the opportunity of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but you refer to it, so therefore I was a bit confused --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, but I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please clarify the matter, if you would.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I think it's clear now, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, who -- do you know who was or were either the representative or the representatives of the Serb Democratic Party, the SDS, referred to in this draft document?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I see here, the president of the Serbian National Council in Bosnia and Herzegovina, that was Mr. Radovan Karadzic. He should be under number 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The -- did you receive a report of discussion relating to this proposal?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: From some conversations I learned what happened there, but I memorised only a little of what I heard. I know some people walked out. I know some people accepted the proposal, and as far as I understood - but I'm not quite sure - this initiative was not entirely successful as a result of the boycott by some parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did this initiative, as you've just labelled it, did it lead on to anything which had any significant impact on the subsequent policies and actions of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you mean the policy of the SDS? Yes, right. You mean the SDS. This body never had any influence that I felt or that I encountered in practice later, and that's why I can say that it did not exist, especially not in terms of actual decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Krajisnik, on the -- we've already seen this many times. On the 12th of July, 1991, there was an Assembly of the SDS on the anniversary of the previous year's inaugural meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have a transcript of that meeting. It's among those hyperlinked and scanned documents. Excuse me one moment. Your Honour, may I hand Mr. Krajisnik a similar document. In a sense it has got the number -- the numbers marked in the margin --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- reference point in the same way. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I was just inquiring whether Your Honours have and if not, whether Your Honours need a hard copy of this item.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have not -- let me just ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you provide us with a hard copy, we will check whether we can find it on our computers at this very moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That would be true with the Prosecution as well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It may well be, but I have not yet logged in on our series of ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, I remind -- Mr. Sladojevic is bringing it up for Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, I'm sorry, I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I again have the blurred version of -- it's -- that's the stenogramme.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I think it's a different button. Mr. Sladojevic tells me that a different button gets pressed. Is it the middle one on the left?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's a better one than the right upper-hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I haven't forgotten Your Honour's request for hard copies of these matters, though on this occasion it hasn't yet been implemented. I do acknowledge that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's proceed for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, could you go, please, to point number 2 in the margin. It's quite a number of pages on. And it's on page 25 of the English version. Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you. And this is -- this is Mr. -- Dr. Karadzic speaking, and he says about ten lines down: "I have to say one thing: We have to preserve the strength of the party, not to give in to power-grabbing impulses and 'little Napoleons' who are trying to do things that will harm the Serbian people. "We did have a regional board, which we had to change. It was in fact in Bosnian Krajina, which had become completely alienated and become a power above the municipal boards." Mr. Krajisnik, can you say who was Dr. Karadzic referring to in his reference to "little Napoleons"?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, he meant little Napoleons, people at the regional level who got to be in charge of the regional SDS policies and grabbed power, elevated themselves, and decided they were independent of our policies, who decided they could chart their own policies independent of the party. And prior to that, Mr. Karadzic put some people on the regional level in charge of coordinating regional boards of the SDS. So these people acquired a certain power and, to put it crudely, abused it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did he -- Mr. Krajisnik, did he clearly have particular people in mind in that reference?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He certainly meant some specific people, but I would have to engage in guesswork as to who he meant. He meant the top people in certain regions that were not social-political communities, as he said, who started behaving in an arbitrary fashion. It would be unfair of me to say: It's this person or that person, because it would just be guesswork. But these were important people in the region. These were not ordinary members. Perhaps the most important ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: He -- when he referred to -- he said: "We did have a regional board, which we had to chance, it was in fact in Bosnian Krajina," were you personally involved in any way in that change of regional board that Dr. Karadzic refers to?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not my responsibility. I did not take part in that. Perhaps that for some reason I attended some meeting of that kind, but that was only within the domain of the president of the party, and I don't know who was involved, if it has to do with Bosnian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Would you turn to -- Mr. Krajisnik, to -- it's number 4 in the margin. It's a couple of pages -- well, it's actually about four or so pages further on, probably. It's page 29 of the English. There's a passage, again Dr. Radovan Karadzic, and just stop at number 4 in your margin. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And if it's the same layout, it's five paragraphs into that contribution of Dr. Karadzic where it says in English: "I have to say here that the policy of the Serbian Democratic Party is not to divide Bosnia and Herzegovina until others bring it to that point. The SDS furthermore does not approve of the creation of new federal units before the constitutional and legal system has broken down." When Dr. Karadzic referred there to the creation of new federal units, what -- did you understand what he had in mind there?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He meant that Bosnia-Herzegovina should be federalised, that is to say, to make one, two, or three federal units, just like Bosnia was in Yugoslavia. There should be a certain number of federal units in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Federalisation would mean legalising a canton or a bigger region through regionalisation but through appropriate parliamentary process.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now where -- but that's -- but that process at that point, Mr. Krajisnik, the creation of new federal units, is -- that was a correct reflection of SDS policy, was it, that the SDS did not approve of creation of new federal units at that point?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is the month of June 1991 and --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, July, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: July, July. July.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I interrupted you just to correct the month, Mr. Krajisnik. You --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And at that time there was a very active debate between the Serb and Muslim sides that was supposed to be crowned with a historic agreement between the Serbs and the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When Dr. Karadzic says here: "I have to say the policy of the Serbian Democratic Party is not to divide Bosnia and Herzegovina until others bring it to that point," had there been discussion within the SDS of at what point the Serbian Democratic Party would switch to a policy of dividing Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that that's a good question, so I'll try to explain. The first part of Mr. Karadzic's answer is the official position at that time of the SDS. There was a left wing and a right wing, and there were many discussions. An answer to those who said: Well, we don't want to break up Bosnia and Herzegovina but it's the other ones who want to break it up. Then he added what he did in order to bring about a political compromise in this political discussion, believing that this would not happen at all. So that was the position of Mr. Karadzic as a politician, to give an answer in advance to those who would later debate the issue. We don't want to do it, others want to do it, so that was the answer that he gave at that point in time in July 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was there a contingent SDS policy at that time for any sort of break-up of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps -- well, I'm sorry. Perhaps the best way of answering would be as follows. All of us advocated maximalist views in negotiations, but we had our reserve positions. Our concept was Yugoslavia, and our reserve position was that if there is no Yugoslavia then we would have our constituent unit in Bosnia and Herzegovina. There was no third option. Intimately some people said: If Muslims want to create their state and the Croats want to create their state and if they want to secede, well, why would we not have a state of our own? But that was not an option that was discussed at the time in Bosnia and Herzegovina at the level of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When you say it was your reserve position, then, that you would have your constituent unit in Bosnia and Herzegovina, do you mean that it was, although not publicly stated, it was -- it was actually a matter of discussion within the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That kind of option was always discussed but as a reserve option; the primary option was for us to remain in Yugoslavia, for Bosnia to remain in Yugoslavia, and for Yugoslavia to be re-arranged, that some institutions be moved to Sarajevo. We were talking about a reformed Yugoslavia. Of course we advocated a Bosnia. We participated in that, too, that is to say, that certain things from Yugoslavia be transferred to Bosnia-Herzegovina. So why -- the only thing we didn't want were borders and passports that would separate us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Krajisnik, this particular session of the SDS, it moved into a different type of session, didn't it, at some point where there were a number of invited guests from other parties and other nationalities. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, because there were guests from other parties at all sessions. All parties were invited, so I believe that it was the case here, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In fact, if you find point 6 in the margin, Mr. Krajisnik. That's page 45 of the English. And then in fact we go on about four or five paragraphs into Dr. Karadzic's contribution there. It's top half of page 46 of the English. Mr. -- Dr. Karadzic says: "We have the formal part of the session here, and I would kindly ask the delegates to remain here after the formal part and then we can vote. Because Messrs. Izetbegovic and Cengic, people from the HDZ will come here. They have invited us, too, and we must pursue the policy of cooperation." And then if we go on, Mr. Krajisnik, quite a long way, about eight or ten pages, do you have point 9?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Which is page 58 of the English, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you have 9, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: There's Abdulah Konjicija, I'm doing my best with that pronunciation, president of the Chamber of Citizens of the Bosnia and Herzegovina Assembly. What nationality was he? He was Muslim, was he?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then the next speaker is point 10, it's middle of page 59, Mr. Rabija Subic. Who was he?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a lady --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, I beg your pardon -- well, I beg her pardon.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not receive any interpretation of that. Rabija Subic was president of the Socialist Party of Bosnia-Herzegovina, if you were asking me about her party affiliation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And her nationality?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Her name is a Muslim one but she was married to a Serb, so perhaps she was a Yugoslav.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Could we go on, it will be about another ten pages, Mr. Krajisnik, to find number 14. It's page 68 of the English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: This is you speaking, Mr. Krajisnik: "Ladies and gentlemen, I'm glad that you have greeted me" -- did I say it was the middle of page 68?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I did say it was page 68, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: "Ladies and gentlemen, I'm glad that you greeted me, and particularly because Mr. Konjicija was the first to get up and Mr. Muhamed Cengic was the last. "I like both of them, they fight for their people with honour, and I for mine, and all those who fight for their people deserve to earn only respect, never criticism." And then you complement previous speakers. And then at the top of page 69 in the English it is, but it is about five paragraphs on into that answer you say: "I am likewise happy that the people in this our party have never asked me to work to the detriment of other peoples because that would have been devastating." And then at the -- in your -- the last paragraph of that answer, I want to read through the whole thing, Mr. Krajisnik, I don't feel that's necessary. But the last paragraph of that -- not answer but contribution you say: "The only thing I can say before this gathering is that I will speak out in support of those things that the Serbian people has authorised me to do. When I'm not able to do so, then I will certainly do so, just as I did a few days ago. All those who know me know that I will sooner convert to another religion than break my word." Mr. Krajisnik, the -- you were -- at this meeting you were elected to the Main Board, weren't you, of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And of course you remained the president of the Bosnia and Herzegovina Assembly throughout this period. Were you -- what degree of direction, if any, did you receive from leading members of the SDS as to what you should say and what positions you should adopt in public?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the positions were generally known and simple, and that's what I said here, that I protect my own people but that I could never work to the detriment of other peoples. So I was chairing the Assembly fairly, I was fairly voting, and I was fairly presenting my views. Within this general milieu, so to speak, there were never any requests put forth to me: You defend the Serb people. I did not have any individual instructions as to: You have to do this or you have to do that. We had consultations. As a witness said here, we had these brainstorming sessions, so to speak. It was actually a reflection of the will of the entire Serb people, and I knew what the people wanted and that is what I propounded. This has to do with the people primarily, not the party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you have an opportunity to clarify the question mark in the part you just read from these minutes where it reads: "When I'm not? Able to do so, then I will certainly do so," which created some ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, do you see it? It's your -- your contribution that starts at margin number 14, and then the very last paragraph of that, the first sentence beginning: "The only thing I can say before this gathering," I read that a few moments ago. Then the next sentence after that in English that begins: "When I am not," I wonder if you could just read out that sense from the -- your Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just have to find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krajisnik, take your time. It's the very -- it's the very end of -- you find marginal point number 14. Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've found it. I've found 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, and then go to the very last paragraphs of that contribution by you. It ends up with: "Thank you. "(Applause)." Do you see, just before the chairman speaks up again. Do you find that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you like me to read it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, please, Mr. Krajisnik. It's the -- simply saying -- read the paragraph that starts: "The only thing I can say before this gathering." Just please read that short paragraph out loud, please.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What it says here is the following. "Before this gathering I can only say that I will advocate to do those things that I have been authorised by the Serb people to do. When I cannot do that, I will, just as I did the other day, certainly do it. Everyone who knows me knows that I will rather convert to a different faith than not keep my word." I will explain what this is all about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, yes, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps, Mr. Stewart, since what Mr. Krajisnik just read, that we first tell him what our problem is in English. The line reads: "When I'm not able to do so, then I will certainly do so," so therefore I have two problems in understanding that if you are not able to do it that you will certainly do it. That's my problem. But if you can explain, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I explained a few moments ago what my mandate was: To work fairly, not to work to the detriment of other peoples, and to defend the interests of the Serb people. That was my mandate, and that's what I said. I thanked the SDS for not having asked me to protect the Serb people only to the detriment of other peoples. That was my mandate. Before this meeting, there was an Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the SDS MPs walked out there. That is what Mr. Bjelobrk referred to here. I stayed on my own with the other deputies. Irfan Ajanovic went out -- or rather, took the floor, and others did, too, and said that they had an objection. They wanted me to be replaced. And I said: All right. I want to have a vote on me straight away. If I'm not fair -- well, they said: Well, there are no SDS MPs. I said: Never mind. Only the HDZ and the SDA were there, and that's what I was alluding to. They were trying to tell me not to do that, but I insisted that they vote only on that. And then when they said: We're sorry. We are not going to ask for that, Mr. Ajanovic started praising me, and I said: Don't praise me any longer. Now the SDS is going to replace me. And that's why I'm saying that I'm going to be asked to be replaced if I'm ever asked to work outside the scope of my mandate. That is what I was trying to say, that I would rather convert to a different faith than not keep my word. That intention of mine, I certainly would have carried it out. This is an Assembly meeting that I was presenting here and that everybody knew about, because you saw this other person here thanking me for having chaired the Assembly in a certain way, and I chaired the meeting, although it was the HDZ and the SDA MPs who were there and the SDS MPs walked out. I said that I would have a vote of confidence as far as my work was concerned if I were not acting fairly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Stewart, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, it looks as if there was just a slip in the Serbian text, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's not fully clear to me yet, but nevertheless I think it's not such a major point that we should spend more time on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I agree, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm looking at the clock. It's 25 minutes past 12.00. If we would have a break now for 20 minutes, we would have one hour remaining.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we will adjourn until quarter to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, I'd like to deal with a very practical matter which also explains why we are later than you would have expected. At very short notice, a plenary meeting of the Judges was scheduled for tomorrow morning. Since at the moment this was announced none of the courtrooms was available in the afternoon, and since the Judges find it very important not to lose any day, if possible. We're trying to seek solutions for that, one of them being a request to the President to be relieved from our duty to be present at the plenary. It is of such importance to us. It now turned out that the Martic case has finished for the week and they were sitting tomorrow in the afternoon. So the latest instruction I gave is to see whether we could use the courtroom used by the Martic case and then move to the afternoon tomorrow. Even Mr. Registrar was not aware yet of that last move. We only saw the Martic Judges seven minutes ago. Would it cause any major problem? And I would like to ask the parties to keep in mind that we found it important enough, if need would have been, to ask the President to relieve us from the duty to be present, would there be any major problem if we would move tomorrow to the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's no problem at all for the Defence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, none for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's -- well, Mr. Krajisnik, you're the witness now so you're in a bit of a different position, although you're nearby and mainly available, but it could have been that you had other matters such as medical examinations or whatever, but I see that you are nodding that it is no major problem for you as well. Therefore, Mr. Registrar, you're invited to seek verification that we could move to the afternoon tomorrow and inform me as soon as possible. Mr. Stewart, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, could you find, please, point 15 in the margin.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, this will be at the top of page 76 of the English. In fact, it's the very bottom of the previous page, 75, in the English. It simply says "Dr. Radovan Karadzic," and then what he says: "Just a few words," at the top of page 76.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, do you have that where Dr. Krajisnik [sic] begins to speak and starts with "just a few words"?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then he says: "We have tested the attitude of the Army and in the past few months we have seen that the attitude of the Army towards all the parties is more or less the same. I will tell you off the record that they recognise that the SDS is a centrist party, not a rightist party, but officially their attitude towards all the parties is more or less the same. We have seen that they have resolved to defend, not the Serbian people, but whoever comes under attack. And that's fine by us. Because we will not be attacking anyone and there is no way and no chance that we would enter into any conflict with the Army." Mr. Krajisnik, the -- this -- this is clearly a pretty public meeting, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were the press present, do you -- can you recall?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. Probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Had you personally been involved in any discussions with representatives of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I had for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What period?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think in the second half of 1991, as the Speaker of the parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I attended meetings with the local commander of the 2nd Military District and the federal officials of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You've just referred to the second half of 1991. I think perhaps my question wasn't specifically clear enough. This meeting we're looking at now is the 12th of July. At this meeting at the time that Dr. Karadzic was talking, had you, up to that point, been personally involved in any discussions with the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I was, but if I had been it could have been only discussions between Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Yugoslav People's Army. I never talked to the Yugoslav People's Army on behalf of my party.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did -- as far as you knew at the time, did what Dr. Karadzic was saying here about the position of the JNA genuinely represent your understanding of the army's attitude?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And Dr. Karadzic continues: "If, however, we come under attack and since the Army is obliged to defend the victim of the attack, then it will have to defend us because it is an important state institution. It is defending those who are under attack in Croatia now. "We have said clearly that we will not be creating any party armies. We know that Serbs are arming themselves with smuggled weapons and some ancient ones. We as a party do not have the right to arm the people, but we do not have the right to discourage it either because we could lead it into a position so difficult that it could result in it suffering." Did you have any knowledge, Mr. Krajisnik, at that time of Serbs arming themselves with smuggled weapons and some ancient ones?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my previous answer I said I really didn't know in which way Serbs were arming themselves, if they were arming themselves. Later when the armed conflict began I saw that they had weapons which meant that even back at that time various communities had been arming themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Then Dr. Karadzic continues: "As for the Army" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters kindly ask the speaker to indicate what is the number of the page in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, perhaps you can help us on that. What page number are we on, please, in your version?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Page 92. 0092 -- the number ends with 722. Right?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's -- there's an internal page number of the document itself. I'm not talking about in an elaborate reference number, just the simple page number.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: 92, page 92.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters do not have that page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, is it one missing page or do you -- doesn't it end in 92? The difference is quite big between what we have, 76, and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have certain pages 90, then we don't have 91, 92, then we have 95. I mean, it's random a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know how this has happened. My apologies. We'll do better tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Next time Mr. Stewart will count all the pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I will personally do it, Your Honour, certainly. Giving the page number and not the page was sort of good news and bad news, wasn't it, really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is -- the interpreters without it, would they like to have re-read the portion just translated or ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We simply ask the speaker to read it slowly, so we will try to do it a vista. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Okay. That's a deal.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So yes: "As for the Army, we have issued an instruction which they resent. We have issued an instruction that all personnel should respond to the first call-up of the JNA. We will not allow the JNA, if it comes under attack in this area, to be defeated and humiliated in our Bosnian crags. This will not happen because the Army is also our Army, as long as it defends Yugoslavia. The volunteers will not be exclusively Serbian. I know that there are volunteers from the" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's only now that -- at least the French translation, which I can follow, has -- so you're invited to slow down even in your pace of reading, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I will then, Your Honour. "The volunteers" -- it doesn't come naturally, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: "The volunteers will not be exclusively Serbian. I know that there are volunteers from the ranks of other peoples in Bosnian Krajina, for instance, in Bosanski Novi there are Muslims who are volunteering to defend the Serbs in Croatia, and I know for a fact that they are taking in refugees and helping provide accommodation and food for them. "So we for our part advise our members to respond to all JNA call-ups. I believe that it would be sensible for other parties who want to have peace to recommend to their members that they respond. We will not be responsible for any imbalance in the ethnic composition of the Army. Those who prevent their party members and members of their people from responding will be responsible. Those who encourage reservists to leave exercises, et cetera."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, all this was being said by Dr. Karadzic in the presence of the invited guests from the different parties and nationalities, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that meeting I believe Dr. Karadzic said that and everybody who attended heard it. I'm now speaking on the basis of this text. He said that in -- publicly at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was there any negative reaction or hostility from any member of any other party or nationality to anything that was said by Dr. Karadzic at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so, but I'm saying this with one proviso. Very often there were individual extremists advocating the creation of a new Serbian army. I'm not sure if on this occasion there was a discussion of that kind. I don't think so, but this was heard by everybody who attended. Because to give you one example, some extremists viewed the JNA as "a communist" armed force.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this point, and it may be a tiny bit in the nature of an experiment, but we hope it will go smoothly, Your Honour. At this point, we would like to deal with one or two intercepts that tie in, and the -- largely the way we're proposing to do the intercepts, though, we'll be flexible, Your Honour, is that -- with Your Honour's permission is I'm going to invite Mr. Josse to deal with those. I hope that's not at all disruptive; it should be far from it, actually. So may I from time to time handover to Mr. Josse at an appropriate point in examination for him to deal with such matters?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, although usually, of course, counsel would -- it would be one counsel that examines one witness. This is -- in view of the length --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Teamwork is not opposed to by the Chamber, but of course a final decision could only be given if the Prosecution would have expressed itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I have no objection at this point. Mr. Stewart points out, it is an experiment. If some matter arises that we think we should bring to the attention of the Court, then we certainly will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then a decision at this point is final. That there is no opposition from the Chamber. Of course what happens in the near future, we will see. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will handover to Mr. Josse then. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, intercepts will be played in a similar way. That means everything in order to get it on the record will be read in English and translated into French so that we have a complete record. And I think the procedure was that where the interpreters almost necessarily are a bit behind, that one is following and reading and the other one is reading the -- or is translating.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, this also is going to be a further experiment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The first intercept that I'm going to take the witness to has not previously been exhibited and I do propose to play it. Quite a number I'm simply going to refer him to without actually playing them. In order, again, to cut down on the welfare of paper, we've got a number of B/C/S versions of the intercept, one of which will of course go to the witness. One will go into the translation booths, as well. The English will be on the screen, and Mr. Sladojevic will follow the audio and bring the text up on the screen accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Nevertheless, here the same is valid as for exhibits. First of all, if we said that we would like to have hard copies of the exhibits, if it's an existing exhibit if we could get a list prior to the hearing, then of course we could try to collect them and bring them ourselves which saves half a wood in copying. Because although I highly appreciate the work of Mr. Sladojevic, he is now at the mouse and I'm not at the mouse anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So I can't scroll back and that's -- so we are losing some of our control, not over the presentation, but on verifying other matters such as going back to the date, et cetera. But let's start with the -- let's start with the experiment and let's see whether it works. And if anyone, either interpreters, technicians, or Judges, parties, or you, Mr. Krajisnik, will have any difficulty with the procedure, I would like to hear from you. Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So, Your Honour, we're going to play an intercept of the 16th of July, 1991. Could one be handed to Mr. Krajisnik. One is going to need to go into the booths, please. There's a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is an unexhibited --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: To the best of our record. We've checked this as thoroughly as we can, and we do not think this has previously been exhibited. Let me also add that all exhibits are as a result of Prosecution disclosure -- I beg your pardon. All intercepts, what I should have said, are a result of Prosecution disclosure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You do not expect any objection as far as their origin is concerned?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would like to be provided with a copy of the B/C/S as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, with a B/C/S copy, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, whilst this is being handed to the final booth, I spoke to that booth, which is the B/C/S booth, and really --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction, English booth.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you, the English booth. And I think they would like some guidance as to what Your Honours would like them to do. Simply to read out this transcript or attempt to translate the intercept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Our experience in the past was that it's impossible to translate it immediately from the spoken word, words spoken. And it's my recollection that we ask some teamwork under those circumstances, one following the B/C/S text and the other one reading the English translation, as it has been prepared, which of course also gives us an opportunity later to check whether the translation is -- whether there are any mistakes in the translation. But that's at least the translation we work on. So actually, it is the written translation that serves us, but at the same time for the completeness of the record, we want those -- this English translation to be read out so that the transcript of this hearing, of this court hearing, is complete.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we should instruct those who are making telephone conversations to speak a bit slower for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd invite this to be played now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Where is the English translation, may we inquire?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We are inquiring as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have to stop for a moment. We expected to have the English translation on our --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So did we.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- but as we see nicely the two children.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I think -- southern Germany, Your Honour, that is. The -- Mr. Sladojevic is having -- it's beyond his control, I can see that. He's having a -- there's a difficulty with the technical connection, I think. He's doing the normal and right thing, and it's just not working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think he'll -- may receive some assistance from our technicians.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have an English translation for the intercept. It is 03219444. We may be able to show it if the Court -- if that would be of assistance to counsel and to the booths.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then perhaps later resolve the technical problems. You could do that through your computer or should we put it on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I will defer to my expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, we don't have it in hard copy, Your Honour, it won't be on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It won't be on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We've called it up electronically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes -- well, at least could it be enlarged a bit and then scrolled in such a way that the interpreters could perhaps read it from their screens. It's rather small. My eyes would not -- well, would have some difficulties in -- yes, that's perhaps better. Is that sufficient? Yes. Let's then proceed. Mr. Sladojevic, if you can --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm grateful to everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It has no exhibit number yet, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D178, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: With the B/C/S transcript as .1 and the English as A.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, let me just check. One question: Are we going to receive this on a CD-ROM? Because the -- intercepts usually are submitted in electronic format and then the transcripts get number A for the transcript and A.1 for the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I discuss that overnight with Mr. Sladojevic, Mr. Haider and also the very helpful technical staff of the Chamber, because we are very reliant on them to help us with that type of production.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps I can even imagine that not a new CD will be burned for every transcript but perhaps at a certain moment that we get various telephone intercepts on one CD which then says: This is D178 up till D -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If we can do that after the event, because clearly I won't make a final decision --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- as to what I'm in fact going to play --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But it's just a suggestion -- and since my children even learned me how to burn a CD, I'm fully confident that Mr. Sladojevic would be -- Let's start. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now we have a problem of which -- I thought before that it's difficult to feed our electronic evidence systems from two different computers at the same time. Therefore, usually we had the intercepts which was a combined text -- combined text and sound CD. We don't have it here. Also perhaps a matter to be further explored by you, Mr. Sladojevic, and to the extent the Tribunal can help you, of course we will, and the same will be true, I take it, for the OTP. At this moment Mr. Registrar offered us to make a printout of the electronic -- of the transcript in English so that that can be provided to the booths so that while playing it we have a hard copy available for the booth. The logistical aspects of these exercises need some more attention as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yeah --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Although I envy Madam Usher for having an opportunity to have some exercise during the day. I would not encourage that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: There's no question about that, Your Honour, I accept that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Registrar, were you able already to make a printout?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We're going to have one try, I think, of playing the intercept and having it up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] Radovan KARADZIC: Both Osijek and all of that up there ... Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Well, your party is really something. There's no other like it. Radovan KARADZIC: (Laughs). Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Do you see the way we work? Listen? Radovan KARADZIC: Yes. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: When you get the Montenegrins and the people from Krajina together, and you yourself come from the old Herzegovina, you can only imagine how it works out. Radovan KARADZIC: Yes. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Professor Bulatovic is here. Those premises ... Radovan KARADZIC: Yes. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: They are there for certain" -- The text has scrolled up out of sight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The text should follow the -- perhaps we stop again. By scrolling you should -- Mr. Sladojevic, you should follow the English interpretation and not the original B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Exactly. That was my fault for giving Mr. Sladojevic the wrong instruction. Precisely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So if we could re-start. At the same time, the teamwork within the booth will not become more easy, but we are in an experimental phase at this moment.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note that the transcript is always read out at a reasonable speed, whereas the actual conversation is as fast as it is. So we do our best, but that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And therefore, Mr. Sladojevic is invited to follow your speed and not anything else. Let's re-start and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] Radovan KARADZIC: Both Osijek and all of that up there should ... at least ... at least the Drava. Radovan KARADZIC: Well, your party is really something. There is no other like it. Radovan KARADZIC: (Laughs). Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Did you see the way we did it? Listen! Radovan KARADZIC: Yes. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: When you get the Montenegrins and the people from the Krajina together, and you yourself are from the old Herzegovina, I can ... you can only imagine how it goes. Radovan KARADZIC: Yes. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Professor Bulatovic is here. Radovan KARADZIC: Uh-huh. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Those premises ... Radovan KARADZIC: Yes? Momcilo KRAJISNIK: They are there for certain. Radovan KARADZIC: Uh-huh. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Will you please -- he only says that the request ... He is going to deal with it but regarding this we should ... We should get together and finish this. Radovan KARADZIC: Uh-huh. Listen. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: For it's complicated. The government doesn't have to do anything. Radovan KARADZIC: It doesn't. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Nothing. Radovan KARADZIC: Great. Shall we -- well, okay, we'll see about it. Listen, Zulfikarpasic was looking for me frantically for a couple of days. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Yes. Radovan KARADZIC: He got me on the phone today. I had been avoiding it all, but he got me on the phone today. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Yes. Radovan KARADZIC: He says we have to meet up, a historically important agreement between Serbs and Muslims is coming into sight. We can't ... I said ... and I said, remember when I told you this. Before our founding convention and you said you wanted to see who would be in the party. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Uh-huh. Radovan KARADZIC: Well, now the chips are down. He says: I also persuaded Alija. He will join all this. We'll meet up today and arrange me a meeting with Milosevic tomorrow. They are in a panic. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: They have to pay the entrance fee. Radovan KARADZIC: I tried to avoid it, but I said I'd meet him for a short while at this. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: That's okay. Radovan KARADZIC: To meet him at Nikola's, so I thought it would be a good that you come and then. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Just tell me at what time. Radovan KARADZIC: Well, around 2.00. I think we should meet there at quarter past 2.00. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Good. Will you ... Radovan KARADZIC: Is it okay with you? Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Well, no, listen, I don't think you can find two guys like Bulatovic and me anywhere. You're okay but you're only the second best. Radovan KARADZIC: Well, I'm honoured to be second best to you. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Huh? Radovan KARADZIC: I am honoured. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Bad politician. You're a diplomat. I must say. Those poor things, those of other denominations, they've got a tough deal to have to cope with you. Radovan KARADZIC: (Laughs). Momcilo KRAJISNIK: I'm kidding. Quarter past 2.00 is okay. Radovan KARADZIC: Okay then. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Listen. You know what we're going to do? Radovan KARADZIC: Yes. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: You know, when you get an assignment, you want to finish it as soon as possible. He and I ... Radovan KARADZIC: Yes, yes. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Somebody from up above, one of our men should write it or we should write a letter on behalf of ... but it should be a memo ... no, it can't. Radovan KARADZIC: It has to be a memo, but over there, those were flooded up there, so they can't enter those ... Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Yes. Let me tell you - this should, I mean ... as soon as possible. Here's what I told him" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Shall we go on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I take it that something -- I don't know whether the original in B/C/S has finished by now?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It has.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It has. So then perhaps we could do without the music and stop that and ask the interpreters to finish the English interpretation and the French interpretation. I expected at least some Yugoslav music under the circumstances, but unfortunately ... the interpreters are invited to read the remainder of the translation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Here is what I told him. He should take care of this. He should say, whenever the HDZ and the SDA ask for it, we'll give them the premises that they want. Radovan KARADZIC: Yes, yes, of course. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: So that the Assembly should act according to this. Radovan KARADZIC: That's great! Excellent. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Will you then please listen to what I suggest? It can, since there is no room up there ... Radovan KARADZIC: Yes. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: I'll definitely meet up with ... to get it over with. Radovan KARADZIC: Okay. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: And we shall assign Mr. Bulatovic, since he makes big sacrifices for our people. Radovan KARADZIC: Okay, that's a deal. And we shall talk before 2.00 so that we can meet at a quarter past 2.00 and then maybe ... finish it. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: And will Alija be there? No, I don't think he will. Radovan KARADZIC: No, no. He said he had talked with Alija and convinced him. Alija would like to be a part of this. He wants Milosevic to see him tomorrow right after the talks with us. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: No, no, he has to earn that. I don't know, we'll see. Radovan KARADZIC: No, we have to analyse. Yes, but first we have to hear ... to get a loan. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Yes, yes, good ... to Bosnia. Good, that's a deal. And what are we going to do about these premises. Please ... just get this over with. Radovan KARADZIC: I'll call down there right away to see if there is anyone to write this ... Momcilo KRAJISNIK: You don't have to. I'll tell you what - I'm going to call Ostojic. Radovan KARADZIC: Yes. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Since little Zoran was there. Radovan KARADZIC: Uh-huh. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: We have to see where he went. Radovan KARADZIC: Uh-huh. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: And we should tell him to get in touch, to write that memo, the request for the premises. Radovan KARADZIC: Uh-huh. And you know what you should do? Call Simovic and Ostojic. Simovic has already had a request like that and it went through ... I mean, since it was ... he had to go through the government. It went through some commissions. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Yes. That is wrong. That is not Vlado's --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: That is not up to the government, or the governments. That is interpreter's correction. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Not Vlado's. Radovan KARADZIC: Yes. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: It belongs to the Centar municipality. Radovan KARADZIC: Uh-huh. It's theirs, for sure. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Here's what I'll do. I'll hook up Simovic and ... I mean Mr. Bulatovic so that the two of them can finish it and there you are. Radovan KARADZIC: Great! Now I'll call Simovic to ... Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Okay. You don't have to do anything. I'll do it all. Radovan KARADZIC: Well, then. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: All of it. Don't worry. Radovan KARADZIC: See you. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: See you. Everything's settled. Radovan KARADZIC: Thank you. Have a nice day. Give my regards to the Professor. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: I will."

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you and Dr. Karadzic are discussing the proposed historical agreement. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The Chamber has heard something about that. There is reference here to Mr. Zulfikarpasic. What was his role in the proposed agreement?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Zulfikarpasic was the president of the Muslim-Bosniak organisation, and they had launched an initiative together with Professor Filipovic to have a historic agreement reached between the Serbs and the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, Professor Filipovic and Mr. Zulfikarpasic were not in Mr. Izetbegovic's political party, were they?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were not. At first they were, but at this point in time they weren't. At the beginning of political pluralism in 1990, that's when they were with him, but at this point in time they were no longer with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What's the name of their political party at this point in time?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The MBO, the Muslim-Bosniak Organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And why were they in the vanguard of the proposed agreement from the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had a proposal for two peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina through their political representatives to reach an agreement and resolve many questions that were controversial ones throughout history in order for a solution to be found for the future as to how they should live together in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The point was for Bosnia and Herzegovina to remain within Yugoslavia and that it remain integral. That was their request and that corresponded to the interests of the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And have you any idea how they presented the matter to the SDA and Mr. Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was present at a meeting, perhaps it was precisely this one at Mr. Koljevic's, when the two of them, Mr. Zulfikarpasic and Filipovic, said: We have a proposal for a historical agreement. And they presented what I said to you a few moments ago. And we also have the support and consent of Mr. Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And it may be obvious, but it's central to the questions I'm asking. Why were you in favour of this agreement?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I shared that view. I wanted Bosnia to remain an integral whole and that it remain in Yugoslavia, and I wanted us to reform Yugoslavia and to find a long-term solution that would lead to peace, that there would be a long-term agreement between the two peoples. Of course the third people would have to be involved, too, and the others as well, but this was an initiative of two peoples that would have been offered to the Croat side as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What was Mr. Milosevic's involvement in it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Milosevic was considered by the Muslims to be the leader of all Serbs, and they would have only been too pleased to have Mr. Milosevic's consent as well. They even thought that we were under Mr. Milosevic's patronage. So if we agreed and he did not agree, that would be an insufficient guarantee for them; that's why they wanted to talk to Milosevic as well, which actually did happen. And this was confirmed by Mr. Zulfikarpasic in the interview he gave to Nin magazine.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What was the relationship between the historical agreement and the Belgrade Initiative?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that it is practically the same thing or there were only technical differences in nuance. This is an interpretation based on that kind of historical agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Why did the agreement and/or the initiative fail, from your perspective anyway?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer is simple. The Muslim side -- or rather, the SDA gave up on the agreement. Of course the Croat side -- or rather, in parliament as well, but the focus here is on the Muslim side. Their role was crucial as personified through Mr. Izetbegovic. He gave up on this. Mr. Zulfikarpasic and Mr. Filipovic said that. They drew back and that's why it went down the drain.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps that would be a convenient moment. We will consider overnight whether to play any more intercepts in relation to this or perhaps some other way of presenting them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that. Before we adjourn for the day, perhaps a few practical matters. Mr. Registrar, if I could specifically have your attention. The Nielsen source material has not received a number, did it?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's four tabs in one binder.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be P1177.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1177. That had been reserved and not been used meanwhile, yes.
